Teaching Begins with Understanding the Learner A clear explanation can still leave students unable to use an idea. More homework can still repeat the same mistakes. How Learning Works asks teachers to investigate what produces these gaps.
Susan A. Ambrose and her coauthors connect research on learning to decisions teachers make each day. Their central argument is that teaching improves when instructors understand how students build knowledge, direct effort, develop skills, and judge their progress. Subject expertise matters, but it cannot replace an understanding of these processes.
This summary covers the 2010 book, How Learning Works: Seven Research-Based Principles for Smart Teaching. Wiley’s edition record confirms the five authors and seven-part structure. Richard E. Mayer wrote the foreword. The book addresses college teaching, although many of its questions also help tutors and workplace trainers.
The seven principles describe interacting conditions. They are not seven steps that every lesson must follow. The teaching examples below illustrate their use; unless identified as book examples, they are examples created for this summary.
1. Prior Knowledge Can Support or Obstruct Learning Students interpret new material through what they already know. Accurate knowledge can provide a foundation. Missing knowledge leaves gaps. Incorrect knowledge can make a new explanation seem wrong or mean something the teacher never intended.
The authors distinguish knowing a fact from knowing how to use it. In the publisher’s chapter excerpt, students report familiarity with statistical tests but struggle to apply them. Recognizing a method’s name does not establish that a student can select and perform it.
Another book example concerns negative reinforcement. Everyday associations with the word negative can lead students to confuse it with punishment. The technical term concerns strengthening behavior by removing something unpleasant. Correcting the definition once may leave the older association active. These examples appear in Wiley’s first-chapter excerpt.
The practical response is diagnosis. Ask students to explain an idea, solve a small problem, or predict an outcome before teaching the next topic. Different problems require different responses. A reminder may activate forgotten knowledge. A missing skill needs instruction. A misconception needs opportunities to examine and revise the underlying belief.
2. Knowledge Needs Useful Connections Students can remember many facts while lacking a structure that makes those facts useful. The second principle concerns how knowledge is connected and organized.
Experts tend to see relationships that beginners miss. A beginner may group problems by their visible features. An expert may group them by the principle needed to solve them. Meaningful connections help a learner retrieve relevant knowledge when the setting changes. Kennesaw State University’s discussion of knowledge organization, adapted from the book and updated for its later edition, explains this distinction.
Consider a student who files every example under its lecture date. That system helps locate notes. It gives little help when an exam asks which ideas explain an unfamiliar case.
Teachers can make relationships visible. Show how a new concept fits the course’s larger questions. Ask students to compare cases or sort problems and explain their categories. A concept map can expose missing or mistaken links. Its value comes from explaining the connections, rather than drawing an attractive page.
3. Motivation Depends on Value and Expected Success The authors treat motivation as a response to goals and circumstances. Students must see a reason to invest effort. They must also believe that their effort has a reasonable chance of producing success. A supportive environment helps sustain that belief.
Value takes several forms. A student may enjoy a subject, care about becoming competent, or need the skill for a future goal. These reasons can coexist. The framework therefore gives teachers more options than trying to make every topic entertaining. See the book-based explanation of student motivation.
Imagine a student who wants to work in public health but believes statistics is beyond them. Explaining its career value addresses only part of the problem. A manageable first task, clear criteria, and useful guidance may help establish a credible route to success.
The teaching question becomes specific: does the student lack interest, confidence, support, or some combination? A demanding assignment can be motivating when students understand its purpose and can see how to approach it. Purpose alone cannot repair missing preparation.
4. Mastery Requires Parts, Integration, and Transfer Complex performance depends on several abilities working together. The authors identify three demands: acquire the component skills, combine them, and recognize when to apply them. Success at one demand does not guarantee success at the others.
An expert can overlook these demands because familiar actions require little conscious attention. This expert blind spot makes it easy to skip explanations or underestimate the time a beginner needs. The book’s framework is developed further in Kennesaw State’s account of mastery.
Consider writing a research argument. A student must evaluate sources, form a claim, select evidence, and explain how the evidence supports the claim. Practicing citation format alone will not teach the whole task. Assigning a complete paper without support may overload the student.
A teacher can isolate a weak skill, then return it to the larger task. Students also need varied situations that require choosing a method. This is transfer: using learning beyond the setting in which it was acquired. Asking students why an approach fits a case helps reveal whether they understand its conditions of use.
5. Practice and Feedback Must Work Together The fifth principle links practice to clear goals and feedback that helps students move toward them. Repetition has limited value when students cannot tell what to improve. Comments have limited value when there is no chance to act on them.
Practice should present an appropriate challenge and occur often enough to develop the intended skill. Feedback should identify relevant features of performance and guide the next attempt. The related practice-and-feedback resource explains this cycle.
For example, a teacher might ask students to explain how one paragraph’s evidence supports its claim. Feedback could identify an unsupported inference and ask for the missing reasoning. Students then revise the paragraph before writing a longer argument.
This is more actionable than a general instruction to improve clarity. It also gives the teacher evidence about whether the feedback helped. A rubric can make criteria visible, but students still need to understand what those criteria look like in actual work. The useful unit is the whole cycle: attempt, information about performance, and another informed attempt.
6. Development and Course Climate Affect Learning Students bring social and emotional concerns into the classroom alongside their intellectual work. The sixth principle connects their development with the course climate. A student learning to weigh competing interpretations may need help moving beyond the expectation that every question has one approved answer.
Climate includes whose contributions receive attention, how disagreement is handled, and whether students can ask for help. Coauthor Michele DiPietro’s discussion of course climate explains how belonging, communication, and selected course content can shape participation and learning.
Imagine a seminar in which a few confident students answer every question. The instructor may interpret silence as understanding. Other students may be uncertain about the material or unwilling to risk public error.
Brief individual writing before discussion can give everyone time to form an answer. Clear discussion rules can make criticism more productive. Teachers can also ask students about their experience instead of assuming that a friendly intention creates a supportive climate. These choices help students engage with difficult work while maintaining academic standards.
7. Independent Learning Must Be Taught The final principle concerns metacognition: monitoring and directing one’s own learning. The authors describe a cycle of assessing a task, judging current knowledge, planning an approach, monitoring progress, and adjusting strategies. Carnegie Mellon’s statement of the seven principles presents this cycle as a skill students need to develop.
An assignment may require comparing explanations, while a student prepares by memorizing definitions. More time with the same strategy may leave the mismatch intact. Teachers can model how they interpret a task and decide what successful preparation requires.
The book includes exam wrappers among its practical tools. These short reflections ask students to connect preparation with results. Students examine how they studied, identify patterns in their errors, and choose changes for the next assessment. Carnegie Mellon provides examples and guidance.
The important change is from vague judgment to specific evidence. A student can replace a conclusion about being bad at a subject with an identified difficulty, such as choosing the right method. That difficulty can guide the next practice session.
Using the Framework with Care My practical reading is to begin with one recurring learning problem. Collect evidence from student work. Then select a response that fits the likely cause. A weak essay might reflect poor source evaluation, a misunderstood task, or difficulty connecting evidence to a claim. Each explanation suggests a different intervention.
The framework’s breadth is also a limit. It does not supply a fixed teaching method or guarantee a particular result. It draws together research from different areas rather than testing one complete instructional package. The original book appeared in 2010; its research discussion should not be treated as a current systematic review.
Its college focus also requires care when applying it elsewhere. Younger learners, workplace trainees, and students with different access needs may require different forms of support. Clear feedback cannot by itself remove every barrier to participation.
The book gives teachers a disciplined set of questions. Its strongest practical contribution is to make student learning something instructors investigate, support, and reassess through concrete evidence.
Sources Wiley: original edition, author credits, and contents. Wiley: first-chapter excerpt, including the prior-knowledge examples discussed above. Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center: seven learning principles and exam wrappers. Kennesaw State University’s book-based teaching resources, linked in the relevant sections, provide further explanations. These pages include later-edition updates; this summary retains the original seven-principle structure.

Learning Means Building Knowledge You Can Use A student can repeat an explanation and still misunderstand it. A class can complete many exercises and struggle when a problem looks different. How People Learn asks what these gaps reveal about learning and how education should respond.
John D. Bransford, Ann L. Brown, and Rodney R. Cocking edited this National Research Council report. Its full title is How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School. The original appeared in 1999. A 2000 expanded edition connected its findings more closely to educational practice. This summary covers the original report’s central ideas, using the publisher’s accessible expanded text to examine them. The publisher’s original-edition record explains this relationship.
The report’s central argument is that education should build usable understanding. It brings cognitive, developmental, social, and brain research into a shared account of learning. Three themes guide its recommendations: engage existing knowledge, organize facts around important concepts, and teach learners to monitor their understanding.
Begin with the Learner’s Existing Explanation Students interpret instruction through ideas they already hold. Those ideas can help them understand a lesson. They can also change its meaning in ways the teacher never intended. A student may learn the expected answer for a test while keeping an older explanation for everyday life.
Teaching therefore needs to reveal students’ thinking. Predictions, explanations, and discussion provide better evidence than asking whether everyone understands. A wrong answer can expose a model of the world that needs careful revision. The report develops this principle in its opening chapter.
This view gives teachers an active role. They must connect new knowledge to existing ideas and help students examine conflicts. It does not imply that learners should discover everything without guidance. Explanation and demonstration remain useful. Their success depends partly on how learners interpret them.
Experts Organize Knowledge Around Meaning Experts know more than beginners, but quantity alone does not explain their performance. Their knowledge has a useful structure. They notice patterns, retrieve related ideas, and recognize the conditions under which a method applies.
The report describes studies in which people sorted physics problems. Beginners often grouped problems by visible objects, such as inclined planes. Experts grouped them by the underlying principle needed for a solution, such as conservation of energy. Similar-looking problems can require different methods. Different-looking problems can share a solution principle. See the chapter on expertise.
This is why factual knowledge and conceptual understanding need each other. Facts give a concept substance. Concepts make facts easier to organize and use. A curriculum made of disconnected details weakens both.
Expert performance also does not guarantee expert teaching. A fluent practitioner may overlook steps that a beginner must work through consciously. Teaching requires understanding the subject and the learner’s route into it. The goal includes adaptive expertise: being able to reconsider an approach when familiar routines no longer fit.
Transfer Requires More Than Repetition Transfer means using learning in a new context. It is a central test of whether education has produced flexible understanding. Performance on familiar exercises may conceal difficulty with this larger task.
The report recounts an early study of children throwing darts at an underwater target. One group received an explanation of how light bends through water. Another practiced without that explanation. Their performance was similar in the practice setting. When the target’s depth changed, the group taught the principle adapted better. This is an example reported in the book, not a new experiment or a guarantee about every lesson. See Learning and Transfer.
Transfer depends on adequate initial learning, meaningful practice, and opportunities to compare contexts. Teaching one example in depth can establish understanding. Varied examples then help students recognize what remains constant when surface details change.
The report also warns against judging learning only through immediate, unaided performance. Prior study may prepare someone to learn from new information, even when it does not produce an instant solution. Assessment should sometimes examine that capacity to keep learning.
Children Are Active Thinkers The developmental research challenges the idea that young children simply wait to receive knowledge. Infants detect patterns and differences before they can explain them in language. Children build expectations, try strategies, and revise their approaches.
Their competence is uneven. A child may reason well about a familiar subject and struggle with an unfamiliar task. Limited knowledge or difficulty with a test format can hide an ability that appears under different conditions.
Adults help by directing attention, linking new experiences to familiar ones, and adjusting the difficulty of a task. The chapter on children’s learning presents development as an interaction between the child and the learning environment.
That chapter also treats metacognition as a developing ability: understanding and directing one’s own learning. Learners need practice setting goals, checking progress, and changing strategies. A useful teaching move is to make these decisions audible while working through a task. Students can then practice the same checks with support and gradually take responsibility for them.
Design the Whole Learning Environment The report describes four complementary perspectives on a learning environment. They concern the same classroom, rather than four competing teaching styles:
Learner centered: Attend to students’ knowledge, beliefs, language, and cultural experience. Knowledge centered: Build accurate understanding of important subject matter and how ideas connect. Assessment centered: Make thinking visible and provide feedback that supports improvement. Community centered: Establish expectations that support inquiry, explanation, and learning with others. Assessment has a particularly important role. Formative assessment supplies information during learning so that teachers and students can adjust. Summative assessment evaluates achievement after a period of instruction. Both should reflect the learning goals. If teaching values reasoning but tests reward only recall, the parts of the environment work against each other.
Community includes classroom relationships and connections with families and other settings. Students need conditions in which they can expose uncertainty and examine errors. Participation also depends on whether classroom practices recognize the knowledge and language students bring. These connections are developed in The Design of Learning Environments.
Effective Teaching Combines Guidance with Inquiry The report’s classroom accounts show why successful teaching cannot be reduced to one method. Teachers need subject knowledge, knowledge of common learning difficulties, and judgment about when to explain, question, demonstrate, or let students investigate.
One account follows teacher Barb Johnson, who uses students’ questions to guide investigations across subjects. A question about living to an old age leads into topics including genetics, history, and probability. The important feature is her ability to connect students’ interests to substantial disciplinary knowledge.
The report explicitly cautions that copying this classroom’s general activities would be insufficient without the knowledge needed to guide them. Inquiry needs intellectual direction. Its teaching examples in history, mathematics, and science illustrate that demand.
Teachers Need Conditions for Learning Too Teachers bring prior knowledge, practical concerns, and different levels of experience to professional development. A standard workshop can miss these differences just as a standard lesson can miss students’ needs.
The report applies its learning-environment framework to teacher learning. Teachers need opportunities to study subject matter, examine student thinking, try approaches, and discuss evidence with colleagues. Feedback and a professional community support this work.
One implication is organizational: improving instruction requires time and support for teachers to learn. Giving them a new set of recommendations does not by itself create those conditions.
Brain Research and Technology Need Careful Interpretation The report explains that experience can change the brain’s structure and organization. Learning continues beyond early development, although some experiences have especially strong effects during sensitive periods.
It also warns against jumping from brain findings to specific classroom prescriptions. Evidence of biological change does not establish which teaching activity will work best. The Mind and Brain chapter asks educators to distinguish findings ready for practical use from claims that run ahead of the evidence.
Technology receives a similar treatment. Simulations can make otherwise hidden processes visible. Communication tools can connect students with experts. Interactive environments can support practice and feedback. These possibilities depend on instructional design and teacher support. The report’s technology chapter evaluates tools through what they enable learners to do. Its examples belong to its period; they should not serve as current product recommendations.
Applying the Ideas with Care Consider a lesson about balance. This is an illustration created for this summary, not a documented lesson from the report. Ask learners to predict which side of a beam will fall and explain why. Compare their predictions with a demonstration. Introduce the role of both weight and distance from the support. Then change the arrangement and ask for a new explanation.
The teacher can distinguish an accurate prediction based on a sound principle from a lucky guess. Learners can compare their first explanation with their later one. The activity becomes useful when those explanations guide the next teaching decision.
The framework still leaves difficult choices unresolved. It cannot specify the best lesson length, sequence, or amount of guidance for every group. Demonstrations, discussion, and practice need to suit the subject and the learners.
The report is also a historical synthesis, not a current systematic review. The later How People Learn II, published in 2018, expands attention to culture, learning across the lifespan, and settings beyond school. Those developments matter when applying the earlier report outside its main school context. Readers should treat its principles as questions for investigating learning and evaluating instruction, with results checked against actual student understanding.
Sources National Academies Press: original edition and publication history. ERIC: original report and the three editors’ credits. National Academies Press: expanded edition, full text and contents. Specific chapters are linked above. How People Learn II: introduction and explanation of the updated scope.
